vignette:
Dr. Manuel Vega is a 62-year-old Latin American psychiatrist who has been practicing in a community mental health clinic for the past 18 years. He lives alone in a small apartment near the hospital, keeps his bookshelves perfectly aligned, and never opens the curtains after dusk. He arrives at work precisely at 7:45 each morning, always a few minutes early, always parking in the same spot near the exit so he can leave quickly if needed.

Manuel grew up in a city that, during the 1980s, was swept by political violence. He had just finished his psychiatric residency when he began treating patients who had been detained and released by the security forces-men and women who spoke in whispers about electric shocks, mock executions, and days spent blindfolded in underground cells. He kept careful records of their accounts, documenting physical and psychological scars. One evening, after a particularly long shift at the hospital, two men in civilian clothes stopped him at the gate. They told him he was needed for a "consultation." He never made it home.

For the next three weeks, Manuel was held in a facility he still cannot describe without his chest tightening. He was interrogated about the patients he had treated, about their political affiliations, about his own loyalties. They used what he had learned in medical school-where to apply pressure, which nerves produce the sharpest pain. He tried to detach, to observe his own body as a case study, but the screaming broke through. When they finally released him, they warned him that his silence was a condition of his survival. Within a month, he had fled the country.

Now, in his clinic, Manuel sees patients with similar histories-refugees and asylum seekers who flinch at loud noises and cannot sleep through the night. He is excellent at his work, calm and precise, but his colleagues notice that he never touches a patient without announcing it first, never stands behind a closed door without checking the lock. During team meetings, if someone raises their voice in disagreement, he goes very still, his hand drifting toward the rim of his coffee cup.

At home, he follows a rigid routine. He checks the deadbolt three times before bed. He sleeps on his back, fully dressed in sweatpants and a T-shirt, and wakes up at least twice each night from dreams in which he is being questioned again-recently the dreams have begun to include the faces of his current patients, accusing him of something he cannot name. He no longer drinks coffee because it makes him too alert. He avoids movies with tension, loud restaurants, and any news about his home country. Last month, a car backfired outside his apartment while he was unlocking his door; he found himself on the ground, his keys digging into his palm, his heart hammering against his ribs for nearly an hour afterward.

Manuel knows the diagnostic criteria. He has prescribed SSRIs to hundreds of patients with similar symptoms. He has explained, with clinical patience, that flashbacks are not a sign of weakness but a memory system stuck on replay. But when he sits alone in his silent apartment, reviewing the day's notes, he cannot apply that same compassion to himself. He tells himself he should be better. He is a psychiatrist. He understands the mechanisms. And yet, every time he sees a man in a dark suit at the grocery store, his throat closes. Every time a patient describes a feeling of being watched, he feels a cold certainty that someone is watching him too.

He has not dated anyone in over a decade. The last woman he was with told him he seemed "haunted." He did not argue. Sometimes, when the silence grows too heavy, he pulls out the small leather journal he kept during his residency-the one with the patient testimonies he had transcribed in careful handwriting. He has never thrown it away. He cannot read it either. He simply holds the closed book in his hands and waits for the trembling to stop.

The clinic's director, a kind woman named Rosa, has gently suggested he take a leave several times. He always declines. The work is the only thing that makes the days coherent. But lately, he has noticed himself forgetting small things-a patient's name, a medication dosage. He writes everything down now, in a small notebook he keeps in his breast pocket, as if he is preparing for testimony he will one day have to give.
